title: California Uber and Lyft Drivers Take Historic Step Toward Unionization
excerpt: The California Gig Workers Union has filed a petition to represent over 800,000 rideshare drivers, backed by tens of thousands of signatures, in what could become the largest expansion of private-sector collective bargaining in state history.
body:
• The California Gig Workers Union filed a petition in May 2026 to represent the state's 800,000-plus rideshare drivers, collecting tens of thousands of authorization signatures in what could become the largest private-sector union expansion in state history.
  • Under Assembly Bill 1340, signed by Governor Newsom in October 2025, Uber and Lyft drivers can unionize while remaining independent contractors — a first-of-its-kind framework.
  • California's rideshare workforce includes a significant share of South Asian and Indian-origin immigrants, for whom the outcome could reshape wages and job protections.
  • A UC Berkeley study found California gig drivers earn a median of $5.97 per hour without tips and $7.63 with tips — well below the state's $16.50 minimum wage.

Hundreds of thousands of Uber and Lyft drivers across California are closer than ever to forming a union, after the California Gig Workers Union filed a formal petition with the state in May to represent rideshare drivers in collective bargaining — a milestone in the gig economy labor movement that could have outsized implications for Indian-origin and South Asian immigrant workers who make up a substantial portion of the state's rideshare workforce.

The petition, filed with the Public Employment Relations Board on May 12, 2026, came backed by "tens of thousands" of driver authorization signatures collected over several months, according to SEIU, the union federation supporting the effort. If the board verifies that the union has met the initial 10% threshold of active drivers, all covered drivers will be notified of the organizing effort. The union must then demonstrate support from at least 30% of active drivers to begin bargaining.

How California Got Here

The path to this moment has been years in the making. In 2020, California voters approved Proposition 22, an industry-backed ballot measure that classified rideshare drivers as independent contractors, stripping them of employee protections like minimum wage, overtime pay, and unemployment insurance. Uber, Lyft, and DoorDash spent more than $200 million on the campaign — the most expensive ballot measure in state history at the time.

https://x.com/nypost/status/2087568359365673304

But by 2025, the political landscape had shifted. Governor Gavin Newsom brokered a deal between organized labor and the rideshare companies, resulting in Assembly Bill 1340, which he signed on October 3, 2025. The law, which took effect January 1, 2026, creates a legal framework for drivers to unionize and collectively bargain while remaining independent contractors — a novel approach that sidesteps the employee-versus-contractor classification battle entirely.

"It has the prospect of organizing up to 800,000 members in the gig economy into the union to give them voice, to give them choice, to give them dignity and a say about their future."

— Governor Gavin Newsom

In exchange for supporting the bargaining bill, Uber and Lyft secured a companion measure, Senate Bill 371, that reduces their insurance coverage requirements — a cost Uber says accounts for about a third of total fares statewide and as much as 45% in Los Angeles.

What's at Stake for Drivers

The numbers paint a stark picture. A UC Berkeley Labor Center study found that California gig drivers earn a median wage of just $5.97 per hour without tips and $7.63 per hour with tips — a fraction of the state's $16.50 minimum wage. Drivers bear their own fuel, maintenance, and vehicle depreciation costs, and face the ever-present risk of "deactivation" — being cut off from the platform without explanation or recourse.

"For more than a decade, we have been fighting to have basic protections," said Hector Castellanos, a gig driver from Antioch who has been one of the movement's most visible advocates. "Today we are one step closer to getting to the bargaining table with the world's largest gig corporations."

Key bargaining priorities are expected to include minimum pay guarantees, protection against arbitrary deactivation, access to health insurance or retirement benefits, and reimbursement of vehicle expenses — protections that employees receive under California law but that independent contractors do not.

Why This Matters for Indian-Origin Drivers

California's rideshare industry relies heavily on immigrant labor, with South Asian and Indian-origin drivers forming a significant share of the workforce, particularly in the Bay Area, Sacramento, and Los Angeles. For many first-generation immigrants, driving for Uber or Lyft serves as a critical economic lifeline — flexible enough to accommodate family obligations and language barriers, but increasingly precarious as fares decline and costs rise.

The unionization effort could provide these workers with a collective voice on issues that disproportionately affect immigrant drivers, including language access on the platform, protection from discriminatory passenger complaints, and safeguards against deactivation based on ratings that can reflect cultural biases.

A National Ripple Effect

California is the second state where rideshare drivers can unionize as independent contractors, following Massachusetts, where voters approved a similar measure in November 2024. Drivers in Illinois and Minnesota are pushing for comparable rights. The California model — backed by both labor and industry — could serve as a template for gig worker organizing nationwide.

The law applies only to rideshare drivers and does not cover delivery app workers for companies like DoorDash. But labor advocates say a successful union in California's rideshare sector would build momentum for broader gig worker protections.

The PERB is expected to verify the petition's signatures in the coming weeks. If the threshold is met, the drive to reach the 30% mark — and a seat at the bargaining table — will begin in earnest.
